title: Envoys from Cush and the Patient God
summary: Ambassadors from Cush, the powerful Nile kingdom south of Egypt, arrive by papyrus boat, apparently seeking allies against Assyria. Isaiah sends them home with a message for the whole world: the LORD is watching quietly from his dwelling and will act in his own time, cutting off the enemy like a vinedresser pruning branches before harvest. In the end this distant, feared nation will itself bring gifts to Mount Zion.
story: After Babylon, Assyria, Philistia, Moab, and Damascus, the oracles reach the southern edge of the known world. Cush was the land of the upper Nile, and in Isaiah's lifetime its kings had become rulers of Egypt as well. Judah's leaders were strongly tempted to rely on Egypt and Cush against Assyria, a policy Isaiah fought for years (chapters 20, 30, and 31). Chapter 18 does not condemn the Cushites; it redirects them. God does not need their alliance to deal with Assyria, and he will act when the moment is ripe. The chapter ends with one of Isaiah's great visions of the nations coming to Zion, and it prepares for the oracle against Egypt in chapter 19.
historical:
Cush (often translated Ethiopia in older Bibles, though it is not modern Ethiopia) lay along the Nile south of Egypt, in what is now northern Sudan, with its capital at Napata. Its kings conquered Egypt in the second half of the eighth century BC, beginning with Piye around 728 BC, and ruled it as Egypt's Twenty-Fifth Dynasty for more than half a century. These Kushite pharaohs, including Shabaka and later Taharqa, opposed Assyria's advance and encouraged revolts among the small states of the Levant. Taharqa appears in Isaiah 37:9 as Tirhakah, marching out against Sennacherib during the campaign of 701 BC. He did not become pharaoh until about 690 BC, so many historians think he led the army in 701 as a young prince and is called king in the narrative by the title he later held; others propose a second, later campaign of Sennacherib.

The envoys of verse 2 were probably seeking to bind Judah into an anti-Assyrian coalition, likely around the time of the Ashdod revolt (about 713 to 711 BC) or the wider revolt after Sargon II's death in 705 BC. Isaiah's answer is consistent with his whole ministry: Judah should not stake its survival on Egypt and Cush, but on the LORD. Sennacherib's army was indeed turned back from Jerusalem in 701 BC (Isaiah 37:36-37), though the Assyrians defeated the Egyptian and Kushite force at Eltekeh that same year, and later Assyrian kings invaded Egypt itself.
cultural:
The Nile was the lifeline of Cush and Egypt, and papyrus boats, light craft made of bundled papyrus reeds, were common on the river. Sea (verse 2) can refer to the Nile itself, which is called a sea elsewhere in the Old Testament. The land of whirring wings may refer to swarms of insects along the rivers, to the sound of sails, or to the Cushite kingdom's reputation for swift movement; the phrase is obscure. The description of a people tall and smooth-skinned reflects how the Cushites were seen by their neighbors: impressive, feared, and foreign in speech. The Greek historian Herodotus, writing in the fifth century BC, likewise reported the Ethiopians of the far south as remarkably tall and handsome, which shows the reputation was widespread.

Verse 3 uses the two ancient means of rallying people at a distance: a banner raised on a mountain and a ram's horn trumpet (shofar). Verses 4 to 6 draw on the vineyard year. In the hot, still days of summer, the grape blossom sets and the fruit begins to ripen, and a vinedresser cuts back unwanted shoots with a pruning knife so the fruit can mature.
literary: The chapter is a short prophetic poem framed by two parallel descriptions of the Cushites (verses 2 and 7), repeated almost word for word. In verse 2 they are the subject of diplomacy, the people to whom messengers return. In verse 7 they are the ones who bring gifts to the LORD of Hosts at Mount Zion. The repetition marks the change. At the center (verse 4) is God's own word, reported by the prophet: “I will quietly look on from My dwelling place.” The images of shimmering heat and a cloud of dew suggest God's stillness and presence at the same time. Verses 5 and 6 then turn the harvest image into judgment: the branches are cut and left for birds and beasts through summer and winter.

outline.t: Woe to the land of Cush and its swift envoys
The whole world is summoned to watch
God waits quietly, then prunes the branches before harvest
Cush brings gifts to Mount Zion

doctrines.note: God is not in a hurry and needs no coalition. He looks on quietly from his dwelling and acts at the right moment, and the great powers' diplomacy does not set his timetable.
Isaiah's message to Judah through this oracle is to trust God rather than alliances. Faith here means waiting for God to act rather than seizing security from the strongest partner available.
The chapter ends with a distant, powerful nation bringing gifts to the place of the Name of the LORD. Isaiah sees the nations not only judged but drawn to worship Israel's God.

words.note: Kush, the land and people of the upper Nile, south of Egypt. English Bibles have often translated it Ethiopia, following the Greek, but it refers to the region of Nubia in modern Sudan. The name also appears in Genesis 10 among the descendants of Ham.

Qav-qav, a rare, repeated word appearing in the descriptions of verses 2 and 7, translated here as powerful nation. Its meaning is uncertain: suggestions include might, a people of line upon line (that is, of measuring and command), or a word imitating foreign speech, hence the rendering of strange speech. The difficulty shows how unfamiliar the Cushites were to Judah.

Qatsir, harvest. In verses 4 and 5 the harvest season sets God's timing: he waits through the heat of harvest and acts before the grapes are gathered. Harvest is a frequent biblical image for the moment of judgment and gathering.

christ: The chapter's link to Christ comes through its last verse. Isaiah sees a people from the ends of his known world bringing gifts to the place of the Name of the LORD. In Acts 8, one of the first converts from beyond Judea and Samaria is an official of the queen of the Ethiopians (the kingdom of Kush of that day, then centered at Meroë), who had traveled to Jerusalem to worship and was reading Isaiah on his way home. Philip explained to him that the passage he was reading spoke of Jesus. Luke does not cite Isaiah 18, but the scene shows the hope of this chapter beginning to be fulfilled: the nations coming to Israel's God through Israel's Messiah. The chapter's picture of a God who waits and then acts at the right time also fits Paul's statement that Christ came when the fullness of time had come (Galatians 4:4).
questions: The Cushite envoys offered Judah a strong ally against Assyria. Why do you think Isaiah sent them home, and what would it have cost Judah to listen?
God says he will quietly look on from his dwelling place. How do you handle times when God seems to be waiting rather than acting?
The feared, distant nation of verse 2 becomes a worshiper in verse 7. Who are the people you find hardest to imagine worshiping God, and what does this chapter say to that?
